current_research_question: You agree a price of €250,000. What does the buyer actually need liquid before completion on the Costa Blanca in 2026 — and why is the answer different for a resale and a new build?
must_establish: The ITP rate in force in the Comunitat Valenciana on the date of writing, with its effective date and whether the rate is set by the deed date or the private-contract date (the general rate on immovable property moved 10% → 9% for taxable events accruing from 1 June 2026, under Ley 5/2025 de 30 de mayo; the 11% rate is RETAINED where the value exceeds €1,000,000, and reduced rates of 3%–8% exist for defined buyer profiles)
The new-build path separately: IVA at 10% plus AJD, and the current Valencian AJD rate

Current notary and land registry scales for a €250,000 purchase, taken from the BOE-published aranceles (Real Decreto 1426/1989 for notaries and Real Decreto 1427/1989 for registrars, as reduced by Real Decreto-ley 8/2010) — and, stated separately as unregulated market prices rather than scales, typical gestoría and independent lawyer fees on the Costa Blanca

Which costs shift if there is a mortgage, and who legally pays which of them: the AJD on the mortgage deed falls on the lender under art. 29 TRLITPAJD as amended by Real Decreto-ley 17/2018 (in force 10 November 2018, while notary, land registry and gestoria costs were allocated to the lender — and the appraisal to the borrower — by art. 14.1.e) of Ley 5/2019 (in force 16 June 2019)

Whether any reduced ITP rate could apply to the buyer profile (under-35, large or single-parent family, disability, gender-violence victim, protected housing) — noting that every housing reduced rate is gated on the property becoming the buyer's habitual residence (and, for the under-35 and VPO rates, their FIRST habitual residence), so the question is not whether the buyer is a non-resident but whether they will actually live there; and that the rate additionally depends on whether the value exceeds €180,000
never_assume: For notary and registry costs use the actual tariff. For lawyer fees there is no official Costa Blanca median — quote a real range from identified providers, or omit a 'typical' figure entirely.
Check whether a current Comunitat Valenciana reduced ITP rate applies to this buyer and property profile before any worked example. Never assume the 9% general rate applies to every buyer.
Do not assume a flat 12% or a flat €280,000 — state the assumption set that produces whatever number is used
Do not assume ITP is 10%; the Valencian rate changed on 1 June 2026
Do not assume the purchase is a resale — new build is a different tax path entirely
Do not assume the buyer pays the mortgage stamp duty; the lender has been the AJD taxpayer since 10 November 2018 (RDL 17/2018)
Do not assume the Valencian rate applies to Murcia-side Costa Blanca-adjacent purchases — the region determines the rate

current_research_question: How does Spain's imputed-income rule apply to a qualifying second home that earns no rental income, how is the taxable amount calculated, and how is the obligation self-assessed?
must_establish: The legal basis in the IRNR (art. 24.5 TRLIRNR, by reference to art. 85 LIRPF) and the imputed base: 1.1% or 2% of cadastral value. Which coefficient applies turns on WHEN the municipality's cadastral values were last revised, modified or determined by a general collective valuation procedure — 1.1% if that took effect in the tax period or the 10 preceding tax periods, 2% otherwise — and not on the size of the property's own cadastral value, nor on a rate each municipality chooses. Where there is no cadastral value or it has not been notified by 31 December, the base is 1.1% applied to 50% of the greater of the acquisition price or the administratively checked value. For 2026 the ordinary 10-year rule governs: the 'revised since 1 January 2012' cut-off in DA 55ª LIRPF was written for 2023, 2024 and 2025 and must not be carried into 2026 without checking. Establish this for the 2026 tax year SPECIFICALLY: art. 85 LIRPF sets the imputation at 2% of cadastral value, dropping to 1.1% only where a general collective cadastral revision took effect in the tax period itself or in the ten preceding tax periods. The friendlier 'revised since 1 January 2012' cut-off sits in DA 55ª LIRPF, and as at 1 September 2026 the consolidated text of DA 55ª in force covers the 2023 tax period ONLY. It was not extended to 2026 — and the 2024/2025 extensions were themselves annulled: Congress derogated RDL 16/2025 on 27 January 2026 (BOE-A-2026-2024) and RDL 2/2026 on 26 February 2026 (BOE-A-2026-4667). For 2026, apply art. 85's ten-preceding-tax-periods test, not the 2012 date.

19% where the owner is TAX-RESIDENT in another EU Member State or in an EEA State covered by mutual assistance on exchange of tax information — which AEAT confirms means Iceland, Norway and Liechtenstein. 24% for everyone else, including someone tax-resident in the UK after Brexit.

That the tax is self-assessed on Modelo 210 with no assessment issued, and the current filing window as amended by Orden HAC/623/2026: for 2025 imputed income, 1 January to 31 December 2026; from the 2026 accrual year onward, 1 April to 31 December of the following calendar year — so 2026 imputed income is filed between 1 April and 31 December 2027
How a part-year rental changes the calculation — imputed for the unlet days, real rental income for the let days
Whether Spanish residents pay an equivalent imputed income on a second home, so the article does not misrepresent this as discrimination
What actually happens on non-filing: surcharges, interest, and the recargo scale
never_assume: There is no routine annual assessment bill: the owner normally self-assesses the liability on Modelo 210. Non-compliance can still bring an AEAT assessment or enforcement, so never say nothing is ever sent.
Never base the figure on market rent, purchase price or valor de referencia — the base is cadastral value

Never apply 24% to an owner tax-resident in the EU or in Iceland, Norway or Liechtenstein, and never apply 19% to an owner tax-resident in the UK. And check that the owner is a non-resident at all — a British national who is tax-resident in Spain files IRPF, not Modelo 210.
Never frame it as a tax only foreigners pay
Never state a euro figure without stating the cadastral value it came from
Spanish tax residents and non-residents can both face imputed-property income on qualifying second homes, but through different taxes — IRPF versus IRNR — with different rates, forms and deadlines.

current_research_question: What LTV and affordability criteria does each named Spanish lender currently publish for this buyer profile, how does the lender classify resident/non-resident borrowers, and does its treatment actually differ between the relevant profiles?
must_establish: Current LTV from named lender sources, split only the way lenders actually publish it: Spanish resident buying a primary residence, versus non-resident. Do not build EU / non-EU / UK / US / Swiss LTV bands — no lender I could open publishes them. Where residence outside the EU changes anything published, it changes the application channel, the documentation and the term available on a non-euro income, not the LTV.
Whether the LTV is applied to the purchase price or to the lower of price and the bank's tasación — this materially changes the cash needed

Establish affordability criteria and LTV from each named lender's current product or underwriting material. If a lender does not publish a threshold, do not invent one. Use that lender's own definition of resident/non-resident — do not silently equate its underwriting category with tax residence.

Term limits published by a named lender for non-resident borrowers — CaixaBank HolaBank caps the term at 20 years for euro and major-currency income and 15 years for other permitted currencies, against the 30 years commonly available to residents. Report an age-at-maturity limit only where the lender publishes one; HolaBank does not, so do not assert one.
Whether any lender exceeds the band and on what condition (existing banking relationship, private banking, nationality)
never_assume: Never state a single non-resident LTV figure such as 60% as the rule — the published distinction is resident versus non-resident and the cap varies by lender, product and borrower profile; Do not assert an EU-versus-non-EU LTV band unless a named lender publishes one — none that I could open does. What residence outside the EU actually changes is documentation and the application channel, plus the term available where income is in a non-euro currency. Enhanced anti-money-laundering checks are not triggered by third-country status as such: under art. 11 Ley 10/2010 they attach to countries on the European Commission's high-risk list, and otherwise on a risk assessment.
Never present 80% as what every resident gets — that figure is for a primary residence

Never assume the reader is British — but the variable is fiscal residence, not nationality: check whether the borrower is tax-resident in Spain, since a Dutch, Belgian or Irish buyer who is not resident is underwritten as a non-resident like any other
Never assume the LTV applies to the agreed price rather than the bank valuation
Never invent a named bank's current LTV or rate

current_research_question: A derrama lands that dwarfs your monthly fee. When can you legally refuse to pay it, when does voting against it change nothing — and can you inherit the previous owner's unpaid share?
must_establish: The exact conditions of LPH art. 17.4: three-fifths approval, works not required for conservation, habitability, safety or accessibility, cost exceeding three months of ordinary common expenses, and the owner having voted against
What falls outside the exemption — conservation, structural safety, habitability and mandatory accessibility works bind every owner regardless of vote
The consequence if a dissenting owner later wants the benefit: paying the updated share plus legal interest
LPH art. 9.1.e: how far back a buyer inherits the seller's unpaid community debt, and the certificado de deuda the seller must produce at completion
Whether the ITE/IEE building inspection regime in the relevant Costa Blanca municipalities can force works, since inspection-driven works are usually non-exemptible
never_assume: Never claim that voting against a derrama never protects you — art. 17.4 is a real exemption with real conditions
Never present the €90 monthly fee or the €8,000 derrama as typical figures; use a worked example flagged as illustrative or a real budget the agency supplies
Never assume the exemption reaches conservation, safety, habitability or accessibility works
Never state the buyer's inherited-debt window from memory — confirm the current LPH wording
Never imply the community can seize the property without describing the actual affección real / judicial process

current_research_question: What does it actually cost to own a €250,000 coastal flat for a year on the Costa Blanca — and what actually differs between a Spanish tax resident and a non-resident owner, given that both are imputed on a second home?
must_establish: Every recurring line: IBI, basura where separately billed, community fee, buildings and contents insurance, water and electricity standing charges, Modelo 210 imputed income, gestor or lawyer fee, alarm or key-holding
How IBI is derived from cadastral value and the fact that the tipo de gravamen is set by each municipality — so the figure must be tied to a named town
Published IBI rates and refuse charges for the specific Costa Blanca municipalities the article names, with sources

Which lines are genuinely non-resident-specific versus paid by everyone. The imputed income itself is NOT non-resident-specific — art. 85 LIRPF imputes a second home to Spanish tax residents as well. What is specific to the non-resident is the vehicle: a separate Modelo 210 self-assessment at a flat 19%/24% with no personal allowances. Fiscal representation is not a standard non-resident cost either: under art. 10 TRLIRNR it does not apply to EU residents, nor to EEA residents covered by mutual assistance, and for other owners it bites only in the defined cases or when the tax office demands it — with one exception that must not be dropped: owners resident in a country or territory with no effective exchange of tax information must appoint a representative simply by virtue of holding Spanish property, without AEAT asking.
Realistic community-fee ranges for the building type described, and what the fee does and does not cover
never_assume: Never invent a specific IBI, basura or community-fee figure for an unnamed property
Never present one municipality's rates as the Costa Blanca norm — Torrevieja, Jávea and Orihuela differ
Never publish a single annual total without naming the town and listing the assumptions behind every line
Never assume the community fee includes lift, pool, security or water without the block's actual budget

Agency input required if real numbers are used: actual IBI receipts and community budgets from the agency's own listings, labelled as coming from named real listings. IBI depends on the municipality's ordenanza fiscal and the individual valor catastral, and community budgets are set by each comunidad, so no public source can supply either. Without that input the piece must run as sourced ranges that say the real figure is property-specific — never as a specimen invoice.

current_research_question: Your price is in euros but your money is in pounds. How far has GBP/EUR actually moved over the last twelve months, and what does that swing add to or take off a €250,000 purchase?
must_establish: The actual GBP/EUR high, low and their dates for the period being written about, from a citable rate source
The sterling cost of €250,000 at two dated rates taken from a named official series — the ECB euro foreign exchange reference rate — calculated rather than asserted, with both dates shown.
Which way the move ran — do not assume sterling weakened; through 2026 it strengthened towards 1.18 by July
The real exposure window: typical weeks between reservation contract, deposit and notary completion on a Costa Blanca purchase
The tools a buyer actually has (forward contract, rate alerts, staged transfers) and the fact that a bank's offered rate is not the mid-market rate
Whether the same exposure applies to the deposit, the balance, or both
never_assume: Never reuse £213,000 and £224,000 — the implied June rate of ~1.116 is below the actual 2026 low
Never assume the pound fell over the period; check the direction before writing the emotional framing
Never quote a rate without its date and source
Never present a mid-market rate as what the buyer will get from a bank or broker
Never imply a forward contract eliminates risk rather than fixing a rate at a cost

current_research_question: How is the 3% payment on account reconciled with the seller's final IRNR liability, when is an excess refundable, and when does additional tax remain due?
must_establish: The legal basis in art. 25.2 TRLIRNR: the 3% is a retención a cuenta against the seller's non-resident CGT, not a separate tax

That the obligation sits on the buyer, who files Modelo 211 and pays within one month of the date of transmission, and what happens if the buyer fails to do it — art. 14.5 RIRNR does not give the seller a remedy: it charges the property itself (afección real, noted in the margin of the register), which bites the buyer.

The seller's Modelo 210 deadline — three months from the end of the buyer's one-month period (RIRNR art. 14.4) — and what actually happens if it is missed: the refund is not forfeited, it can still be claimed, and the right to claim it prescribes only after four years (LGT art. 66.c).
The current non-resident CGT rate on the gain, and a worked case where the 3% is less than the tax due so the seller owes more rather than receiving a refund

What the Agencia Tributaria actually requires for the refund: a Spanish NIF/NIE (or, failing that, the Código Identificativo AEAT issues for the purpose), and a bank account in the seller's OWN name — which may be held at a bank in Spain or abroad (if the refund account belongs to anyone other than the taxpayer, it must be open in Spain). A fiscal representative is not a general requirement: TRLIRNR art. 10.1 imposes one only on contributors not resident in another EU Member State, and then only in defined cases (operating through a permanent establishment, the arts. 24.2 and 38 situations, or when the tax administration so requires given the amount and characteristics of the income or the ownership of Spanish property) — and it does not apply to residents of EEA states outside the EU where mutual-assistance rules on exchange of information and recovery are in place, which covers Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. On timing, no official processing-time statistic is published; the only official benchmark is LGT art. 31.2 — after six months AEAT owes interés de demora, without the taxpayer having to request it.
Who pays plusvalía municipal on a sale by a non-resident and whether the buyer can be made liable
never_assume: Never say the buyer's lawyer 'keeps' the money — it is withheld by the buyer and paid to the Agencia Tributaria

Never assume the 3% is refundable or non-refundable merely because there is a gain. Compare the 3% payment on account with the final IRNR liability: any excess may be refunded and any shortfall remains payable.
Never guarantee a refund timeframe
Never assume the seller made a gain — the reclaim story only works where the gain is small or the property sold at a loss

Never assume the 3% is calculated on anything other than the agreed consideration ("la contraprestación acordada") — normally the price declared in the escritura. It is never taken on the cadastral value, the valor de referencia, or the seller's gain.

current_research_question: Your children inherit the Costa Blanca house. What do they actually have to pay, and by when, before they can sell it — and does the Valencian 99% relief reach heirs who have never lived in Spain?
must_establish: The Comunitat Valenciana ISD bonificación for Groups I and II — 99%, in art. 12 bis.1.a of Ley 13/1997. Ley 6/2023, de 22 de noviembre introduced that 99% figure, but it is no longer the current instrument: art. 12 bis was re-enacted by Ley 5/2025, de 30 de mayo, whose DT 2ª redaction has governed since 1 June 2026, with a further redaction due 1 June 2027, and letter c has since been amended again by Ley 3/2026, de 29 de junio.

Whether non-resident heirs can apply the regional rules, and on what connecting factor: LISD Disposición adicional segunda (inserted by Ley 26/2014 following CJEU C-127/12 of 3 September 2014, and amended by Ley 11/2021, de 9 de julio, which removed the EU/EEA restriction and so extended the right to third-country residents by statute). Tribunal Supremo 242/2018 is the case law that forced that change, not the authority to cite today.
The ISD filing deadline after death, the available extension, and what genuinely blocks registration or sale until settled
Plusvalía municipal on an inheritance: who pays, how it is now calculated, and the municipal deadlines
The heirs' own country's inheritance tax (UK IHT, Dutch erfbelasting, Belgian succession duties) and what double-taxation relief exists — often the larger bill
Whether a Spanish will and a choice-of-law declaration under EU Regulation 650/2012 changes what the children face
never_assume: Never assume non-resident heirs are confined to state ISD rules — the regional bonificación is generally available to them, including outside the EU
Never present a large Spanish inheritance tax bill on a Valencian property passing to children as the default outcome
Never extend Group I/II treatment to siblings, nieces or nephews — Group III is on a different and changing schedule
Never assume the heirs' home country charges nothing, or that a Spanish relief removes a UK or Dutch liability
Never invent a euro figure for the estate or the tax without stating the property value and the region

current_research_question: Can the community come after your new flat for the previous owner's unpaid fees — how far back can they go, and what has to be in the file before you sign?
must_establish: The exact current wording and limit of Art. 9.1.e LPH — the part of the current year plus the three preceding natural years — confirmed as still in force at generation date, with the BOE consolidated text as source.
Whether the liability is real (against the property, capped at its value) or personal against the buyer, and what practically happens to a buyer who refuses to pay.

What the law actually requires at the notary: the seller's certificate of being up to date issued by the community secretary with the president's approval, whether the buyer can expressly waive it, and what else conveyancing practice adds.

Whether a derrama (special assessment) approved before the sale but billed after it transfers to the buyer, and how the statutory test decides it: LPH art. 17.11 makes derramas for improvements the liability of whoever owns the property when the instalments become EXIGIBLE — when they fall due — not when the junta approved them.
Whether IBI and other municipal debts attach to the property in the same way, and how that regime differs.
never_assume: That the buyer pays the whole historic debt regardless of age — never state a look-back period without confirming it in the current statute.
That there are three certificates; the count is invented — report the documents the law and Costa Blanca conveyancing practice actually require, however many that is.
That €5,000 is a typical or representative figure — treat any amount as an explicit hypothetical or drop it.
That the same rule covers properties outside a comunidad de propietarios / horizontal property regime, or rústica plots with no community.

current_research_question: The pool isn't on the deeds — is that a paperwork job or a reason to walk away, and how do you tell which before you offer?
must_establish: The distinction between the pool never being declared/registered (declaración de obra nueva) and it never having been licensed by the town hall — these are separate problems with separate fixes.

Art. 255 TRLOTUP sets a 15-year restoration period from total completion under art. 255.1, while art. 255.5 removes that limitation for the categories listed there, including specified public-use land, public domain, protected cultural-property situations and suelo no urbanizable. Check separately any applicable coastal-servitude regime.

Whether declaración de obra nueva por antigüedad is available at all — under TRLSRU art. 28.4 it is only available once demolition can no longer be ordered, which under TRLOTUP art. 255.5 never happens on suelo no urbanizable or protected land — and what it requires: certification from the Ayuntamiento or a competent technician, or a notarial descriptive act, or a graphic cadastral certification evidencing the completion date, plus a Registrar's check that no disciplinary anotación preventiva burdens the finca and that the land is not demanial. No official or professional-body cost range was located; give a cost only if a named Spanish source supports it, otherwise omit it.
What a mortgage valuer does with unregistered square metres — whether it blocks the sale outright or only reduces the amount financed, forcing the buyer to find the gap in cash.
Any secondary consequences: cadastral regularisation, back-dated IBI, and whether an undeclared structure is covered by home insurance.
Separately, establish what TRLSRU art. 28.4 requires for a declaración de obra nueva por antigüedad.
never_assume: That the villa becomes unsellable — cash buyers and regularisation both exist; establish the actual mechanism of harm before claiming one.
A national prescription period (the widely repeated "six years" is not universal) — the Valencian rule and the land class decide it.
A number of documents or a time to check them; drop "three" and "five minutes" unless the research produces exactly that.
Invented town hall fees, architect fees, or notary costs.

current_research_question: You paid to reserve it and now you want out — is that money gone? And if the seller is the one who walks, what do they actually owe you?
must_establish: The legal difference between a reservation contract, arras confirmatorias, arras penales and arras penitenciales, and which the courts presume when the contract is silent — citing a specific Tribunal Supremo judgment by number and date from CENDOJ, not a law-firm summary.

Whether art. 1454 CC applies automatically or only where the parties' intention to allow withdrawal is clear — answered with a named Tribunal Supremo judgment (number, date, recurso) obtained from CENDOJ, not from a law-firm article.
Who typically holds a reservation deposit on the Costa Blanca — the agency or the seller — and what that means practically for recovering it.
Whether Spanish consumer law on abusive clauses can strike down a blanket non-refundable clause in an agency-drafted form signed by a consumer buyer, and any recent case law.
The buyer's remedies when the SELLER withdraws under each regime: specific performance and damages under confirmatory arras versus double return under penitential arras.
never_assume: That the seller must return double — that is one regime among several and depends entirely on the wording.
That a reservation deposit is refundable, or that an agency reservation form constitutes arras at all.
That €6,000 is a standard reservation amount; treat it as an explicit hypothetical.
That the outcome is settled — courts decide these case by case on the contract's terms, and the copy must say so.

current_research_question: Will squatters take your holiday home while you're back in Manchester? Before answering, open the Ministerio del Interior crime statistics for 'ocupaciones ilegales de inmuebles' in Alicante province, quote the count, the reference period and the publication date, and compare it against the provinces where occupation is actually concentrated. Do not state a risk level — high or low — without that figure in hand.
must_establish: The legal categories — allanamiento de morada (CP art. 202) versus usurpación (CP art. 245) — and where a foreign owner's regularly used holiday home falls. Note that art. 245.2 CP applies only to an immueble 'que no constituyan morada', so the morada / non-morada line is the whole question; whether a regularly used second home counts as morada is decided case by case and must be backed by a citable Tribunal Supremo judgment before it is asserted. On immediate police action, apply the flagrancy definition in LECrim art. 795.1.1ª. Establish what flagrancy actually requires under the LECrim and the Interior protocol, since Spanish law attaches no fixed-hour rule to it.

What LO 1/2025 actually changed from 3 April 2025, per category: violent usurpación (art. 245.1 CP) and allanamiento can enter the juicios rápidos route where its conditions are met, but Fiscalía General del Estado Circular 1/2025 confirms non-violent usurpación (art. 245.2 CP) remains a delito leve on the minor-offence track. Establish the realistic timeline for each, and note that there are two separate 15-day periods inside the juicio rápido and neither is an eviction deadline: art. 800.3 LECrim (unchanged by LO 1/2025) is the window for setting the initial trial date, and art. 802.2 LECrim (rewritten by LO 1/2025, in force 3 April 2025) is the window for re-listing a hearing that could not be held or finished. Both presuppose the case qualifies for the juicio rápido at all, which art. 245.2 CP does not. 802 LECrim is a deadline for RESCHEDULING an oral hearing that could not be held — not an eviction deadline.

Occupation figures for Alicante province or the Comunidad Valenciana from an official source — Ministerio del Interior crime statistics, 'ocupaciones ilegales de inmuebles' — quoting the reference period, the publication date and whether the data are provisional, and comparing them with the provinces where occupation is actually concentrated. Do not publish any occupation figure that was not read off that series.

The factors that genuinely move risk: whether anyone visits or key-holds, whether the property looks lived in, utilities left connected or cut, alarm with verified response, and the separate problem of a non-paying tenant (inquiokupa), which is a civil matter and behaves differently.
What Spanish home insurance anti-occupation cover actually pays for, versus what buyers assume it does.

Which official Interior crime or offence statistics actually capture unlawful occupation affecting homes — allanamiento and usurpación where published — at what geography, and what can and cannot be inferred from those figures about the risk to a second home?
Use the exact category label the current Interior or Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad publication uses; do not assume an umbrella category name that the statistics do not publish.
never_assume: Never convert a raw provincial count of occupation incidents into a probability that a buyer's home will be occupied. A high or low risk statement requires a defensible denominator matched to the same geography, period and legal category. If no compatible rate can be constructed, report the incident count and its context without turning it into a personal probability.

Never state that Spain now evicts squatters in 15 days. Keep two things apart. First, since 3 April 2025 Ley Orgánica 1/2025 has added allanamiento de morada (CP art. 202) and usurpación (CP art. 245) to the juicio rápido catalogue in LECrim art. 795.1.2ª, letters i and j — so those offences are on the fast-track list. Second, that is not a 15-day eviction deadline: non-violent usurpación under CP art. 245.2 carries multa de tres a seis meses, which under CP arts. 33.4.g and 13.4 makes it a delito leve tried by the delito-leve procedure, and the fifteen days in LECrim art. 802.2 is only the outer limit for re-setting a juicio oral that could not be held on its scheduled day.
That there are exactly four factors — the count is invented; report as many as the research supports.
That eviction takes years (pre-2025 framing) or that it now always takes 15 days (the reform's target, not a guarantee).
Statistics published by alarm or security companies — use official crime data or say the data is unavailable.
A local incident, a client's experience, or a named urbanisation; if the agency wants a real case in this post it must supply it, with the owner's consent and identifying detail removed.

current_research_question: The developer goes bust before your off-plan flat is finished — what actually decides whether your money comes back?
must_establish: Which regime applies by date: Ley 57/1968 governs off-plan purchases whose contractual relationship arose before 1 January 2016 — it was repealed with effect from that date by disposición derogatoria tercera of the LOE, in the wording given by disposición final 3.4 of Ley 20/2015 — and disposición adicional primera of the LOE, as amended by Ley 20/2015, governs from 1 January 2016 onward. Neither text contains a transitional rule keyed to the date individual sums were paid, so do not present the cut-off as a payment date.
When the developer's duty to guarantee actually starts — on obtaining the building licence — and what, if anything, protects money handed over before the licence is granted.

What the individual guarantee or insurance certificate must contain, and how a buyer independently verifies it is genuine with the issuing bank or insurer rather than trusting a PDF from the developer.
The mandatory special dedicated account requirement, and Supreme Court doctrine on the depositary bank's own liability where it accepted buyer funds without a guarantee in place.

What happens inside a concurso de acreedores: the buyer's creditor ranking, whether the guarantee is claimed against the insurer or through the insolvency, and typical timescales from a sourced Spanish reference.
never_assume: That one document settles the outcome — the special account, the bank's liability and the insolvency route can each change the answer.
That Ley 57/1968 is current law; it was repealed with effect from 1 January 2016 and citing it as live is a dating error.
That pre-licence payments are covered by the statutory guarantee.
Recovery rates, percentages of buyers repaid, or timescales that the research has not produced; €80,000 is illustrative, and no client's off-plan story may be invented.

current_research_question: How close to the sea is too close? What the Ley de Costas can actually do to a property you own on the coast — and what you get if the boundary moves.
must_establish: Whether the dominio público marítimo-terrestre is public domain by law and the deslinde merely declares an existing boundary — establish and state the accurate mechanism instead of an expropriation framing.

What an owner receives when land is incorporated by a deslinde revision: not an automatic 75-year concession. Under disposición transitoria primera of Ley 22/1988 the owner becomes the holder of a right of occupation and must APPLY for the concession within one year of approval of the deslinde; the concession runs for thirty years, extendable by another thirty, free of canon, respecting existing uses and entries. Seventy-five years is the statutory ceiling on any concession (art. 66.2) and on the prórroga introduced by artículo segundo of Ley 2/2013, which is likewise granted only 'a instancia de su titular'. Then set out what the concession does and does not permit (sale, inheritance, mortgage, works, renewal), each against a cited provision.

The servidumbre de protección — 100 metres as standard, 20 metres for land already classed urban when the 1988 law took effect — and what it actually restricts, since it touches far more Costa Blanca buyers than the DPMT itself.

Which regulatory text is in force at generation date, given the Tribunal Supremo annulled RD 668/2022 for omitting the public consultation stage; confirm whether RD 876/2014 in its original wording applies.

must_establish: The Registro de Agentes de Intermediación Inmobiliaria de la Comunitat Valenciana under Decreto 98/2022 (DOGV nº 9405, 16 Aug 2022; in force 16 Oct 2022) is public, free of charge and obligatory (art. 4.1). A working public search does exist and is linked from habitatge.gva.es as 'Registro Público de Agentes de Intermediación Inmobiliaria'. It searches by PROVINCE and MUNICIPALITY ONLY — there is no search-by-name or by-NIF field — so a buyer browses the list for their town and looks for the agency in it, rather than typing the agency's name in.

Before publishing any guarantee, insurance or qualification requirement, confirm the current post-TSJCV 706/2024 position from CENDOJ and DOGV, and whether an appeal or replacement regulation has changed it. Do not reuse the annulled fixed minimum figures unless current law has reintroduced them.

National limb: there is NO national qualification requirement for estate agents in Spain — art. 3 of Real Decreto-ley 4/2000 provides that the activities listed in art. 1 of Decreto 3248/1969 'podrán ser ejercidas libremente sin necesidad de estar en posesión de título alguno ni de pertenencia a ningún Colegio oficial'. Regulation is autonomic, which is why the Comunitat Valenciana register exists at all. Murcia limb: the Región de Murcia has NO operative register a buyer can check. Art. 54.2 of Ley 6/2015, de 24 de marzo, de la Vivienda de la Región de Murcia provides that a registro de homologación de agentes vinculados con el sector de la vivienda will be created, 'cuyas características se desarrollarán reglamentariamente' — but as of September 2026 no reglamento has been approved; the development has been stalled for years despite having gone out to public consultation, and in July 2026 the Colegio Oficial de API and regional deputies were still publicly demanding that it be activated. So a Costa Cálida agency cannot be register-checked the way a Costa Blanca one can. Say that plainly, and never imply an equivalent Murcia register exists.

No published Generalitat data on compliance rates, inspections or sanctions under Decreto 98/2022 was found. State that plainly rather than estimating a compliance rate. The editorial caution stands and is independently well founded: art. 3 of RDL 4/2000 means estate agency is a free profession nationally, and the TSJCV annulled Decreto 98/2022's fixed solvency minimums in December 2024, so absence from the register is a reason to ask questions, not evidence of fraud.

Quantify a trade-off whenever a source actually observes the relevant dimension. Purchase costs a buyer must hold back are law-verifiable and must be given by named component. On a resale: ITP at the Comunitat Valenciana rate in force — 9% general for hechos imponibles from 1 June 2026 (10% before that), but 11% where the value of the immovable transmitted, or of the right constituted or ceded over it, exceeds one million euros, and that 11% applies to the whole value, not just the excess (art. 13.Uno, Ley 13/1997, as amended by art. 33 Ley 5/2025); reduced rates exist for defined buyer categories, so the band must be read off the actual value rather than assumed. A resale purchase deed pays no gradual AJD on top — art. 31.2 TRLITPAJD excludes acts already subject to TPO — so never add both. On a new build: 10% IVA (art. 91.Uno.1.7º LIVA) plus AJD, at 1.4% from 1 June 2026 (1.5% before) under art. 14.Cuatro of Ley 13/1997, but 0.1% under art. 14.Uno.a where the first copy documents the acquisition of the buyer's vivienda habitual as defined in the state IRPF rules — so the AJD rate must likewise be chosen from the buyer's actual use of the property and never quoted flat. Plus notary and land-registry fees and legal fees. These rates are set by autonomic law and move: check the consolidated text of Ley 13/1997, or the ATV's own rate page, on the day of writing. Renovation and reform costs are a different kind of claim and must not be handled the same way: no official statistic publishes 'realistic reform costs on the Costa Blanca'. The nearest Generalitat-linked reference is the IVE's Base de Datos de Construcción (unit construction prices and a €/m² execution-cost module; free viewer, full base by purchase or subscription), which is a construction-price reference, not a record of what buyers actually pay. Any reform figure must come from real quotes supplied by the agency or a named contractor, must be labelled as such, and must never be presented as an official statistic.
